title: Quadratic Form
body:
A **quadratic form** is a function that is second degree in every term and has no linear or
constant part:

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}x_ix_j
$$

$A$ is always taken **symmetric**, which costs nothing (split any cross term $c\,x_1x_2$ as
$c/2$ into each of $a_{12}$ and $a_{21}$) and buys the [[Spectral Theorem]]. In two variables:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x_1 & x_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ b & c\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}
= ax_1^2 + 2bx_1x_2 + cx_2^2
$$

## Definiteness

Classify the form by the sign it takes for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$:

| Class | Condition | Eigenvalues | Surface |
|---|---|---|---|
| Positive definite | $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ always | all $\lambda_i > 0$ | bowl, minimum at origin |
| Positive semidefinite | $Q(\mathbf{x}) \geq 0$ | all $\lambda_i \geq 0$ | bowl with a flat valley |
| Negative definite | $Q(\mathbf{x}) < 0$ always | all $\lambda_i < 0$ | dome, maximum at origin |
| Negative semidefinite | $Q(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ | all $\lambda_i \leq 0$ | dome with a flat ridge |
| Indefinite | both signs occur | mixed signs | saddle |

**The eigenvalue column is the test.** Substituting the [[Spectral Theorem]] and changing
coordinates to $\mathbf{y} = Q^T\mathbf{x}$ removes every cross term:

$$
\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y} = \lambda_1y_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_ny_n^2
$$

A sum of squares with the eigenvalues as coefficients, so the sign of the form is nothing but the
signs of the $\lambda_i$. This is the **principal axes theorem**: in the eigenvector basis a
quadratic form is diagonal, and the eigenvectors are the axes of the ellipse or hyperbola it
draws. It is [[Basis|choosing the right basis to make a hard problem easy]] once more.

Two shortcuts worth having: a $2\times2$ form is positive definite exactly when $a > 0$ and
$\det A > 0$, and **any $A^TA$ is positive semidefinite**, since $\mathbf{x}^TA^TA\mathbf{x} =
\|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 \geq 0$. That second one is why the normal equations in [[Least Squares]] have
a minimum rather than a saddle, and why the singular values in
[[Singular Value Decomposition]] are real and non-negative.

## The second-derivative test

**This is where the course meets multivariable calculus.** For $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$,
the second-order Taylor expansion near a critical point is

$$
f(\mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_0) + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^TH\mathbf{h}
$$

where $H$ is the **Hessian** of second partial derivatives, symmetric by equality of mixed
partials. The linear term vanishes because the [[Gradient]] is zero at a critical point, so
**the local shape of $f$ is a quadratic form and nothing else**:

| Hessian | Critical point |
|---|---|
| positive definite | local minimum |
| negative definite | local maximum |
| indefinite | saddle |
| semidefinite | inconclusive, look higher |

In one variable this collapses to $f''(x_0) > 0$ means minimum, which is the familiar test with
$n = 1$. [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] takes the same criterion from the
[[Multivariable Calculus]] side; the two courses arrive at one test from opposite directions and
neither restates the other.

It is also the reason optimisation cares. [[Gradient Descent]] converges quickly on a positive
definite bowl and badly on one whose eigenvalues differ by orders of magnitude, because the
condition number $\lambda_\max/\lambda_\min$ is the ratio of the ellipse's axes and the descent
path zigzags across the narrow one.
